segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Appreciate you coming here. First, as we start, let me tell you why we’re doing this. You know that they go to school here. Kids this [gestures] way, adults this [gestures] way. One day they’re going to start listening to this, good Cherokee speaking. And also, your children, at some time, when me and you pass away, your children or your grandchildren, they might want to hear you speaking. And if they come here and ask they will let them listen to you talking. As we start, tell me your full name in English.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: It’s just Tom Duncan.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Now in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: ᏔᎹ ᏛᎩ.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: ᏔᎹ ᏛᎩ ᏔᎹ ᏛᎩ do you know what a ᏛᎩ is?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: I don’t really know what it is, it’s just Duncan.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where were you born?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Hastings Hospital here in Tahlequah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How about growing up?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Towards Stilwell. Bell. Bell community, I grew up around.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How many were in your family?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Eight.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What was it like there, in Bell growing up when you all were kids?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: There was a few of them, four of them I think, that were siblings, my parents. We lived close by.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: All of y’all?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Our relatives, cousins. We were all together, even at church mostly. We played around, all day outside. We just ate things like that, that grew in the woods. There were a lot of things back then that you could eat from the woods. That’s what we mostly did. Sometimes they would take us to town. We didn’t hardly go to town.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When y’all were in the woods, did y’all eat things that were in the woods?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Y’all were playing around?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: We were playing around.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What could y’all play, that y’all were playing?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Mostly we just ran around. Cowboy-western like that, cowboys and Indians. We went way on the mountain, when we were growing up there. There was a good place to play because it was rocky. We just did that and also tag and just different things and also at nighttime... what are they called lightning bugs?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: What are they called in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: We’d chase those, or we’d stick them on each other. And if someone was standing over there, we would see him, because he would have them stuck to him. You couldn’t not find something to play with back then.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did y’all have play guns?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: No, we didn’t, but towards the end they gave me one at school. As for me, Have Gun – Will Travel, you know, that Paladin. One like that they gave us at school. That gun he had, that was a Derringer. It came with it. If I still had it today, it would be worth a lot nowadays.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, really.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, really.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: I was proud of it. But we also had those we made of wood sometimes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did all of y’all speak Cherokee?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, all of us.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When y’all gather together, do you all speak Cherokee?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, all of us.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How about when y’all were playing?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Also that. That’s all we knew. It wasn’t till recently we learned a little bit. We just got better at it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you go to school at Bell?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you already speak English when you started?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Just a little but, I did speak a lot.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You learned there.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: We lived near there, just about a quarter of a mile.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Was a bus already going by there then?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, but I never rode it, because it was close. I would just go on foot.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you just like to walk?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, I just liked it. They never did give us a break, even when it snowed. We kept on walking, even in the snow.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Nowadays, even if they see a little bit of it flying around.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: They think it’s good to just sit around nowadays.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It was the same thing when I was going to school. Just a little bit. They would barely say, “We’re not having school tomorrow.”

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Back then we didn’t have a lot of clothes, you know, and shoes. They gave us some once a year and if they break, we patched them up with wire.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did they not give you all boots?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, it was like that. But we didn’t know we was that poor. We still really enjoyed it. Seeing each other gave us joy.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So y’all were never starving.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: No, we weren’t. We didn’t have a lot and that also … That oldest brother of mine, mostly liked to cut wood. Sometimes when those geese were flying around. They would shoot one of them, but mostly it was rabbits and different things. Squirrels and birds. Different things we ate. Did you like geese? I didn’t really like it. It was OK, I'd eat it. Have you ate?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Just the smell when they were cooking it, I couldn’t do it.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: That’s what happens to me. We ate it pretending it was meat.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you said y’all lived close by, did y’all depend on each other?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, something, for instance salt or sugar things like that. Or flour, different things like that, we borrowed from one another. You wouldn’t think now that was the way me and you came through, but that was the way it was back then. We depended on each other.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Neighborly, huh?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, they were ready.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They were ready then.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: And then, also we just lived in a two-room house. They would spend the night, I don’t know how we did it. They would be scattered everywhere on the floor, you know. We felt good, there wasn’t anything bad about it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you finish at Bell?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you finished there, what did you do?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Then Stilwell.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you finish there?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: I didn’t finish there. I went to the military. I went to the eleventh grade. I finished the eleventh. When I went in there, I finished my GED in the military, in there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where did they put you?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: The basic training?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Fort Polk Louisiana. When I left from there, Ft Eustis, Virginia, then what we were going to do, they taught us that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What did they do to teach you?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: They taught us to lead in the water. I didn’t know the army have ships. Like the people that are in the ships, landing crafts, that’s what they taught us, to the ground.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where they can go?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Where they can go, things like that. I was a crew member.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Was it not when Vietnam was going on?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Back then, I went in from 1969-1971. We had orders to go to Ft Lewis Washington, then we were supposed to go to Vietnam, several of us. We got to Ft Lewis Washington. We were there waiting to go across. And where we came from, Ft Eustis Virginia, orders came from there, while we were there. They were to go back that way. I just missed it, by a little bit.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, you didn’t go then.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: I just missed it, by a little bit. I’m thankful for that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s true, ain’t it? They went through some bad things.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Even when they came back from fighting, they treated them bad.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: They didn’t welcome them, ain’t it? When I think about it, I’m thankful that I was in there, you know, because that is helpful now. If you’ve been in there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How many years were in there?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Two. They drafted me. Back then they were drafting them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I passed the physical, but just after that, they stopped drafting.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: So, you dodged it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: That Levi.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: We went in there at the same time, Levi Gonzalis. We’re good friends even to this day. We were together, through the whole time.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, they didn’t put y’all in different places.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: But when us two got down in Fort Polk Louisiana, we separated. And him… They gave all of us haircuts. Short. He got a haircut first. And when he was coming, he looked like a buzzard. He didn’t have any hair.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I guess his name will be buzzard now.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, tell him that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s interesting! Don’t say anything, he won’t know why we’re laughing at him.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: He could’ve said that to me then. I got a haircut. Yeah, we had a good time. If you know someone, it’s good. It’s also kinda lonesome, because I had never really been that far, you know.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, you were just around Bell.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, and also we were fed. I was enjoying getting fed good. And some were little more upper class.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They did like it.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: They wasn’t liking. Boy, I was really enjoying it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you was there, where that call a base, did they let you go, for instance, to town?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Not in basic training, one time because… You also can’t even eat between meals.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Snacks.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, snacks, nothing like that. One time, there’s this boy, he was a white boy. We were in line to eat. And you had to walk by where that was cooking. And there was these beautiful bananas laying there. We had field jackets on. We got one each.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You two were stealing.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: We got caught.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How did they charge you two?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: They took us towards where the captain was sitting. We were holding those bananas. Captain said, “Y’all peel the bananas. Eat them up in two bites.” That one that was with me, he didn’t take a very big bite the first time. I realized the captain really meant it. I took a bite of half of it. And that other one, he barely put the rest in his mouth. He left too much of it because he didn’t think that captain was serious. That was funny, we got charged with that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And that was it. What was you doing on the plane?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: For the most part we was training the others to do that and I was already settled in.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You were already finished. So, the new ones was coming in and y’all were training them?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, that. We had it made because we had our own cook. We ate real good. We had a big freezer. There was a lot of food in it. And we would just snack whenever we were ready, you know. When you learn the basic training, it will be good. And at that time, they will let you go for the weekend.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Go home.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: And me, I don’t drink, and I’ve never drank. But them boys, we became friends, most of them white, they would take me to town. Even if they were drinking, I would just play pool. They would give me pop and everything. When we were all together.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, it was good. So, when you finished and got out, what did you do?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: I went to school at Okmulgee Tech for electronics. And then I finished in 1975, I think. I was already married to Lucinda. And we had one girl.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And what about... how many kids do you have?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: We have two, one boy and one girl.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do they speak Cherokee?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: They understand it, but I guess if they have to, they might talk.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Let’s go back to that. What did you do when you finished, where did you work?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: When there became an opening, I wanted to go back to Fayetteville, Arkansas, but they already hired someone. And then they wanted another tech in McAlester. I went to McAlester and we stayed there for two years, I guess. When I was working there, they gave me a company car. I was going far and went all the way to Poteau. I was fixing TVs for about two years. I came back to Tahlequah, but really it was Hulbert. We found a place to live. The guy named Hare in Tahlequah, hired me. I don’t know, for about many years.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you like... did y’all like it in McAlester?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: We really liked it. And there was Choctaw I think there, nation right, I think. They were really friendly. When you would use their clinic, they didn’t mind it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They allowed you Cherokees.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: While we was living there, our baby was born there. But he was born in Talihina at the Indian hospital, where it was. Then the oldest girl was born in Muskogee, not here. They weren’t born in Tahlequah or Stilwell.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you have grandchildren?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, I have three. A girl and a boy. The girl we have, had those. Delmar is his name, Littledeer. They still live in Norman. That’s their oldest son, he lives in San Antonio. Now our son has a daughter in Oklahoma City. They graduated from OU, all of them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s amazing.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: They still live over there to this day. But the boy lives over here.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, you have to be for OU.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: I guess.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They played a joke on me at church in Bible school.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: What?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Wednesday, no it was Friday. Thursday night, tomorrow night. If we get 75, will you wear the Texas shirt and the Texas hat? Just 59 we had at first. I didn’t think we would get that many, but it ended up being 89.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: When are you going to put them on?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I already did on Saturday. When we finished, we had activities. John Flute preached for us. And when we finished, we had activities and games and all that, that’s when I put them on.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Were you walking around with those on?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I’m [unclear]

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Was it that burnt orange?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah. What did y’all’s dad do to provide for y’all?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Oh, the principal, Felix Eads at Bell hired him on to work.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: At the school?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: No, just for himself, working around his house. The oldest one, Roger was hired at Bell as a janitor, just things like that helped us out. At that time, even with a dollar a day you could make it. To buy food or a lot of different things.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It was cheap back then.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Gas, I know, back then… I think it was six cents back then, gas.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And when I think about it, it was 24 cents.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You could put four gallons in and it was good.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: If we had a five-dollar bill or if we had... we would run around all night long. About three... or if you just put three dollars in. I’ve seen a lot of people putting in 25 cent worth of gas. That’s what I’m saying six, seven cents a gallon was good.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Like this thing sitting here was probably five cents back then. And I remember telling them... Do you remember Leon Bunch?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He would come over. They lived behind the house. He would say, “Let’s go to the store,” and we would go down the hill. Do you remember Earnest Scraper’s store?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Us two would go there, and if I had a quarter, I would get a pop, chips, and a honey bun.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, and me too. There used to be a store there in Bell. Mrs Worley had a store, and like you’re saying, if you just had a quarter, you could get a bologna sandwich, chips, and a pop.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And Leon would buy four Vienna sausages and then the juice. That’s all he would drink. And me, he would give the sausages to me. And I could only eat about two of them and now the rest, the third one, I couldn’t eat.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: It was pretty cheap back then, can huh, about two or three cents.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: A lot of times I sold pop bottles and I had money from that.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They paid two cents a pop bottle.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: And me, when I was about seven or eight, we started picking strawberries, you know. And still these days I’m wearing Levi’s jeans because they started being $2.50. After picking strawberries, I would buy them. And at the strawberry festival I would have $20. And new…

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: $20 was a lot.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: A lot of them was wearing new clothes and I was, too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You could tell it was time for strawberries. The baseball shirts and a lot of us would wear hats.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: And the radios were really big back then, right? I don’t know if y’all were alive or not back then.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Batteries.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: The batteries were big, too. They were taking care of the batteries. They would let us listen to it. And they listen to the Grand Ole Opry on Saturday nights, if it was Saturday. I remember when I first seen the transistor radio. We were picking strawberries at the house, where John Matthews lived who planted. That Carl Locust, do you remember him?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: He had that in his pocket, that transistor radio. That was the first one I seen. We was impressed with it. So, these days we have phones.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Phones took over.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: That’s right, as well as children. As what we’re talking about, doing things outside like tag and different things like that, Annie Over, things like that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It’s passed away.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: It’s passed away. I don’t know, I guess it’s supposed to be like that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about your mom, did she just watch around the house?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: I was just three when she passed away. I really don’t remember her. My siblings raised me, and our dad raised us.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did he have a garden?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, he really, really had garden back then.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Back then they planted big gardens. Was his big?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, he planted a big garden. He had two mules.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They pulled.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: He used them to plow different things.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And you were too little to help.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, I just walked behind.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You were just in the way.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, I was just in the way.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, I tried that one time. It pulled my legs out from underneath me. I stopped it – now someone else.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: It’s not easy. I tried it, too. They’ll jerk you around. You have to struggle. They worked hard back then. Also canning different things.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, you don’t remember your mom?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: No, but my sisters did.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, they did that, canned stuff?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Plant potatoes?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, different things.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Like what?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Corn, too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What did he do to preserve those potatoes?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: We had a place. We had a building. We would store a lot in there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Same with corn.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Was he drying the corn?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, mostly back then.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What did he use them for when they were dry?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: From what I remember, hogs and chickens.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He had hogs?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, and chickens. They scraped them off and fed them to the chickens.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did y’all kill the hogs?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, and chickens. We felt excited when we were going to kill a chicken. Then when they taught me to cut its neck, I would feel sorry for it to do that to it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Let’s go to Walmart.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: But the food was good back then. Things like that, they would make dumplings and different things like that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I think the dumplings are better if you just now killed the chicken.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, very much so.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s the most flavor to me.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yellow poured in [yellow broth]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I don’t like biscuit or corn bread, but if it’s light bread.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, the dumplings.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: For me, even it’s a biscuit.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I was telling Dad, “Why do we eat biscuits, it already has bread in it?”

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Same with potatoes. You could cook those a lot of different ways. We just ate things like that, and sometimes they would make something sweet. We felt like it was good to eat.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did they learn to cook?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where did they learn to cook? Did they learn themselves or was your dad teaching them?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Just both, they were learning themselves, too, and also Dad could cook good.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I was also nine years old when Mom passed away.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you know Joyce? Well, first, Dad was a good cook.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Is that right?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: “After a while you need to learn,” he told her. And then Dad taught her, to cook. But the first time the biscuits were this big, this thin.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: The biscuits were stuck.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, but she went on to learn. When y’all killed a hog, did y’all waste anything?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Too much.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Y’all used it all?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Even those feet they cook even. That I guess you can still find those today.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Sometimes you can find them.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: My dad is always cooking those.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Is that right?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Ahhh.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about the intestines? Did y’all use those?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Us, when we killed one, we didn’t use those. But I have seen others kill one and use them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They would clean them.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: They would clean them. But we didn’t work out.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I remember a little bit, my aunt and mother would clean them.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, they would reach in there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They would use sticks to turn them inside out.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Some people really like those.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: What about chicken feet?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: They used to cook those. Also like, for instance, the dumplings, we were talking about, some would be in there and sometimes I would take one out and suck on it.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: My dad still buys those and cooks them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: A lot of them just boil them.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Probably just to get the flavor is why they put them in there. I guess we all just lived like that, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: The white people will frown upon things like that, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Those slickhead mushrooms, the white people didn’t know anything about how you could eat them. They raise them themselves now, different kinds of mushrooms. As for me, my wife tells me, “You don’t even hunt. You don’t even look for things like that, but yet, you really like things like that.” But people will bring me things like that because they know I like things like that. But sometimes, I do look.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Does your wife like things like that?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, she’s a good cook, too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Seems to be.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Y’all know me!

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about... Did y’all look for things that were edible from the woods, or who looked for things like that?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: We did most of it, but I remember my sister Ann, we would look for a lot of different things.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Like mushrooms, you said, that together…

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Or also, wild onion, poke salad, different things…

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Uyvhvd [wild bean vine]

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, uyvhvd, the plant, vine, bean vine…

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you like that?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It’s gone away, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, a lot of things have gone away. You used to be able to find wild strawberries – have you eaten that?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, when I was pastoring at Hillside. Have you ever been there?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: No, but I know where it is.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It was at the entrance. The parking lot was like this [gestures]. There was a lot of it hanging there, but it wasn’t sweet.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: It wasn’t?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: No, it got this [gestures] big. It was really red. Boy, I thought it was gonna be sweet when I picked it, but it wasn’t.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: A long time ago, it was sweet, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, there’d be a lot of it.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: What about what they call for rabbits to eat? Have you eaten that?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: It’s about this [gestures] big. It’s like wild cherry. It’s about that size, hanging in the woods. It’d be on the side of the road. I’ve ate a lot like that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How did they cook that?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: You didn’t, you just ate it right there when you picked it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh, so they didn’t cook it.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: No, uh-uh. No.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Was it sweet?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, it was sweet, and also Kanig. [Black Haw Tree]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh yeah, that I do.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Do you know what that is?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: This One [gestures] is too young to know that.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: She’s too young. It’s not just one berry, it's a cluster of them. It didn’t grow as one, it’s bunched up. We go to Branson every year. There’s a road by the lake where you can walk. There’s one plant there, we peek at it all the time every year.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Y’all don’t pick it?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: No, it’s not ripe yet when we go over there. It probably ripens somewhere around September.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about wild grapes, how long has it been since you’ve seen them?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: A long time ago. But like we said, you used to be able to find them anywhere in the woods.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Back then, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: And Possum Grapes, and those have gone away, too, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: For me, last year, there’s a guy named Mike Taylor who lives behind the house. My horses got out and they went over there. He’s a nice guy, he told me, “Do this when you go get them.” And then I went on a four-wheeler, and I had feed on there. I was driving them back and then they stopped. I parked in the shade, and I was drinking water. I was looking around. He has a road there, there was a pine tree over there. I thought, “Man there’s a lot of pinecones on it.” It looked kind of strange. When I looked good at it, man, it was full of wild grapes hanging there on the tree! Boy there was really a lot of them.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Were they already ripe?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Did you pick them?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I went and told the owner, and he said, “Alright, I’ll make grape wine!” I thought, “Ha!” but he called me back and he asked if my wife knew how to make jelly. “Yeah! She makes it every year,” I told him. “Come pick it,” he said. “Make some jelly and we’ll split it. But it was high.” I got a tractor, and he said, “Use that tractor.” It wouldn’t start, the battery was dead, he came back and started it. He put me in that bucket, and we picked all of it. Filled up two trash bags this [gestures] big, full.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Do you think they’re going to come back every year?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I don’t know. He hasn’t said anything yet.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: “I’m gonna be watching out, and if they’re hanging there, I’ll let you know,” he said, but he hasn’t said anything yet.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: You’re going to have to remind him. He might’ve already forgot.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: But she did can 58 half pints of jelly.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Y’all have one?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Or two!

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I have one. If I see you, I’ll give it to you! But also, I told them we have your jelly now…

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: One time, I canned a 100 cans of jam, strawberry. I thought, “Why am I doing this?” I canned 100, I took it to my youngest boys' wedding to give to the people to take. Herb’s son had a case and he walked by, I said, “Hey!”

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When he came to get them, he said, “I just want 12” and he took 12.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Boy, it would just be beautiful everywhere a long time ago, ain’t it? What about the juice from the possum grapes? Boy, the juice was really delicious, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I didn’t like it.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: But cream, I would really eat it.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Me, a while back, about a year ago, George Bunch, somebody gave him some, and he told my wife to make some. He gave us a little bit of that liquid. I really took a big drink of it. He was at a ball game, he was over there drinking that, he took that drink.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Things like that from the woods, did they preserve that?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They canned it.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Nowadays, nobody knows how to do that, the younger generation. But I guess it would cost you less to go to Walmart, but now it costs quite a bit there, too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: My wife knows how to can and preserve, but the first time, there's 12 jars in that box. We used to just pay six or eight dollars for it. Now you’d pay over 20 dollars for it.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, everything, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: The other day, I found some at a yard sale, and I bought all of them. I paid very little for them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I buy them at an auction; you can pay very little there. I’m going to go again this evening.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Where do you go?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Stilwell.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: In the back of...

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah there...

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Behind Means Furniture?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: If you turn by Means, back there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: So, it’s there?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, they start at three o’clock. They start selling inside and when they’re done inside, then they start selling outside. I go over there. What about when y'all get sick, did they take y’all to the doctor or did your dad know a little medicine?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: He did know, but there were also others there that were healers as well. They would go get one of them. As for me, my grandma’s name was Dolly Puppet – I don’t know if you’ve heard of her?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, I’ve heard of her.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: She was my grandma. She was really a healer. They did know roots, too. Back then, they really did know, but we’ve probably lost it nowadays.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I was taught something, Saturday, not this Saturday but a week past Saturday. We were talking about things like that, and we wound up talking about blood pressure getting high. There’s one, we call Yogi, his name is Roy Sanders. He said there’s one [plant] way there in the back. That’s medicine. It’s red and has a sour berry. I don’t know if they call it sumac.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: When it’s like this [gestures] on top, a little bit, it has a red berry.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Red! They told me that. We went and got some, and I told them, “I’m going to try it.” You ain’t even supposed to say that. When you say you’re going to try it, you’re already starting to doubt it. If somebody gives you medicine, you’re supposed to say, “I’m going to use it,” he told me. “OK, I’m going to use it,” I told him. They really did know, and they knew where it was, too, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Did you try it?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Not yet.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: What do you do, boil it?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, boil it.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: I think I have seen somebody do that before.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, you boil it, I was told.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Those like that, they’re sour ain’t they? We used to suck on them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Me too. We used to do that, too.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: And also they used to call sour, it was like grass. We used to eat that, too.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Is that clover?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, that.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: We used to eat that, too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It used to bloom.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: It used to bloom, yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: We used to try to outdo each other. “Who is gonna have the ugliest face?” we used to say to each other.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: It’s been like that ever since.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It never went away, it was like that forever. We used to do things like that when we were going up.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: And also, cherry trees were everywhere in the woods. What about...What do they call in English, ᎤᏍᎫᎩ? ᎤᏂᏍᎫᎩ?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Boatball.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: That’s boatball? We used to eat those, too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Me too.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Those were kinda green. Not the ones that were kind of long. But you could eat the others.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That boatball had something white inside of it. This One [gestures] don’t know what that is.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Uh-uh, I don’t know.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Eat one.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Bring me one.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It was good, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Especially if one is hungry. We was far away from our house you know, that’s why we just ate things like that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you know of them? You know Woodrow Proctor.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And Jim Proctor. Them, sometimes we would skip school. Me and Jim Proctor would go to Woodrow’s house. We would go hunting all day. We would go far away. That’s the kind of stuff we ate, blackhaw (ᎬᏂᎩ). By eating that it was helpful to us.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Especially like till the evening.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And if we found water, we would drink it, but nowadays they’d discourage you to.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: You could drink water anywhere back then. Also, we’d go pretty far if we were going fishing or hunting crawdads. At that creek by Bell. Way out there, I don’t know, about six or seven miles we would go.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Y’all wasn’t thinking about how far y’all would go.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: It was funny to us.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: But when it was time to come back.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: You’d be frowning.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: We would have squirrels and they’d be stiff when we got back.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: And also, you would put that much effort into wanting to kill a squirrel back then. You would even cut a tree down. You don’t [do that now]. We just did that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Just with an axe.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, it was hard work.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Sometimes, we’d smoke one out back then.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: It might come out, then we would be chasing it when it jumped off.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And if a rabbit was to go in and if it was close, we would do this [gestures] and twist it and we would pull it out. That’s what y’all did, too.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, we did.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Like you were saying, if you were starving you were going to do things like that.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: And what about these things that have come out? They call them cicadas or something. What are they called?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: What are they?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: ᎥᎴ.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: ᎥᎴ. Have you ate them? I tried it once.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They say they’re good.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: They alright. They taste a little like crawdads. But I like crawdads the best.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Especially if you just now get them out.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Boy, that really is. You could eat big. It was the best. It was good growing up and remembering things like that. It was hard for us, but we didn’t know it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: But, we didn’t know it. Let me ask you this, when you think about what you were talking about, would you like to go back to that time when you were going up?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Sometimes I think about that, to go back. How good it was where we’ve been. But I don’t know, now I know how bad off we were. When I think about that, I don’t want that. Even though things cost so much now, it’s still easier to find you know. To go back then and thought I enjoyed it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What’s the most treasured thing you think about when you think about it?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: What do you mean?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you think about it, what do you think about the most?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: I guess the church, we lived about Bell school and we went to Salem Church. We had a road just down the hill for a shortcut – we didn’t have to go all the way round. The most memorable for me is just going places and seeing what I’ve seen on earth and done different things. Council, army. I also had my own business. I don’t know if you remember, I had my own TV shop.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh, OK, yeah.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: And starting with that, I tell them what stands out the most and it gives me the best feeling to think about. One time they chose me at Salem Church, when I was about seven or eight years old, to be the bell ringer. That’s what stands out in my life. The reason for that is that they trusted me out of all the kids. But the reason for that is doing something for God, but there isn’t really one thing that is better than the other.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Whatever you can, ain’t it? We look at it as more... what can you say? More important thing, some of it. When God looks at it, it ain’t like that.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: It’s all the same.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It’s all the same.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Just like if someone just recently just started following God, and someone has been following God for 20 years, it’s the same.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Let me ask you this, what year was it when you learned to play music?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: I was nine. They gave me, like, a play guitar. It had rubber nylon strings. That’s when I began to realize I was already interested in a guitar. When a person was playing, I was really captivated. When I would get back after school, I would know where it was at and get there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It just had nylon strings.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Since that time, they gave me one a little better – guitar.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you teach yourself or did someone help you a little bit?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Roger, my oldest brother, helped me a little bit and also Gwid Eli. He knew a little, that one. But for the rest of it, just myself.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where now… that you remember, how long have you been playing?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Let’s see… 65 years. Just like these glasses I have on, this guitar is similar. It’s just like a part of me.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: You might think the same way, too, and say, “Where’s his guitar?” That’s how people relate me to that, no matter where I go, they’ll say, “Where is his guitar?” I don’t sleep with it – I don’t sleep with it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, you remember your guitar instead of your wife.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: That Jerry Wayne Cochran, last Saturday, I told him if I don’t play guitar for a while I get kind of lonesome. I like playing music. He told me, “I guess that’s why I’m always so lonesome, cause I don’t play.” And he don’t even know how. I told his wife to give him one.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, you’ve went back to Salem now, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I guess you play there all the time.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: In 1965 the Lord helped me. I was baptized then. I remember... January 20th 1965. It’s been a long time.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Since you’ve been playing music in a church.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: When I was growing up, before I went into the army, we kind of had a rock band. I can name them, Sundown and Jerry Daughtery. ‘Boss,’ they called. And Charlie, Levi Soap, they used to call him a boy. Me and Sundown are the only two left.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And the others have passed away.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Now me, I’m the only one left of our family. And also, one of these days it will be our time.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And me too, now it started. Just last week, we buried one, my sister last week. Three, four passed on.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: And also my cousin, Walter Jr, he’s the only one that’s left. And now ᏚᏥ, that’s the one that ᏬᏟ raised and Walter. And our dad’s name is ᎤᎶᎩᎳ.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about your mom’s in English?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Flynn.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Flynn.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, ᏚᏥ they call her and Betty Lou and Winnie, are the only two left. And Taylor is the only one left… Whitner… What’s the name of that little town towards?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It’s not Hulbert, is it?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, Hulbert. There is only, like, one of each family that is left.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: But we’re all headed that way, ain’t it? If the Lord don’t come back, that’s what is going to happen. I don’t believe it’ll be that long left to go.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Different things are happening. It’s like, if you know a little about the holy book. If you watch what’s happening on earth, you can use that example or it will reveal how it’s gonna be. It’s just the same as watching the TV in real time.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I’ve seen you sing with a lot of people. Have you got up there and sung by yourself?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, I can sing a few songs. Mostly at the church.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I’ve never seen you do that. Like you said, at churches especially.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Things like helping people out. I did a lot of that. I did a lot of that, setting up. I used to like helping someone. When they take up collections for someone. I can still do it, but there’s not a lot of people who make an effort in that way, ain’t it? It’s going away, as well as singing. When we were going up there would be about three at the same time. If you went to that, then you’d go from there to where the others were singing.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When we had a good group, we would start on a Thursday evening, all the way up to Sunday we’d be going. Nowadays, they’re still there, but they don’t want to do it as much anymore.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: But, this next generation, I guess you could say they’re too lazy.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I want to have an event at the Greasy community building to invite about three groups, maybe every two months, but they don’t do that anymore, do they?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: They don’t, but if someone starts to host something like that, we would support you.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: But I don’t know if I want to, they might call me blue eye.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Since we’re talking about things like this, I’ll tell y’all, at Salem, this Friday at 6.30 we’re going to start singing. Whoever wants to come, can come visit us. When is Gary supposed to preach over there?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Eighth, ninth, and 10th.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Next month?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: We’re ready to go help you.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Alright, that’s good.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: If God lets us.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Us, we are growing.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Is that right?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When we first started, it was hard to get 20 people to be there. Now this Sunday, there was 54 of us there.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: That’s as good as you can get!

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: There’s a lot. Just the other day, one came back. Yogi is his name, that’s what we call him. His name is Roy Sanders. He said he’s been gone 28 years, he came back and took responsibility.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: It’s a great joy when they do that, because nobody is going to find anything good in this world. It’s mostly toward the bad where we’re at now, I believe.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: The way us Cherokees believe, I don’t know if there’s that many left – they call them shape shifters. We know them as sgili [boogerman]. Have you seen anything strange like that?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: I’ve never seen anything like that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You haven’t?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Like that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Have you heard anyone talk about that?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s the way we grew up, but as for myself, I did see something strange. It wasn’t like that, it was God’s work that I seen.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Tell me a little bit about it.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: One time, I was coming from Westville around midnight. When you leave from the Rodeo Ground, where that curve is, that turn off is to England Holler. Where that curve is, we were coming from Westville. I was coming from there. I was really sleepy, and I could really tell that I was sleepy. I was listening to the radio, and there at that curve I fell asleep, I guess. That radio turned up as loud as it could go. When I woke up, I was on the other side of the line, and a car was coming right there, and I managed to dodge it. The radio had never done that before, and it never did that again.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: After that?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: That had never happened again.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Boy, you got woke up.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: He woke me up. We’re not going to leave until God clearly says that’s enough. He won’t let us go until we’re clearly, individually finished. It’s all different, but that’s what I feel amazing about. I know what God has done.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s true.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: He really did use that radio for an alarm system. It wouldn’t do that, would it?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: On its own, you know?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He can do it though.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, God can. It could’ve been an angel that turned it up. When I get there, I’m gonna ask Him.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You’re gonna tell Him you appreciated it!

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: We just lack a little bit. What about what they call Little People? Have you ever experienced anything like that?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: I don’t know if they were talking, but I heard a little bit like talking. When we lived by Bell, in the evenings, you could hear things like that. From them talking about it, they brought them from North Carolina to watch over the houses, they brought some of them. I’ve heard things like that. But I haven’t seen them for myself, but strange things happened like that, it kind of sounded a little bit like people talking.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: For me, a while back, there was a boy that came through that we talked to, and I asked him, he said they got him lost. That’s what they’ll do, they say. He said he went to the woods, then he got ready to go back, he started experiencing things like that. Things were happening like that. He said he could see his house. “I could see my house clearly, but I couldn’t get there. I couldn’t get back. I could see it, but I couldn’t get there. But after a while, something little happened. It was almost like it said, ‘You have to go this way’.”

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: It was just like he woke up.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, it was like that! “I got back to my house pretty quick,” he said. “And I looked back, my house was just right there, but I couldn’t get there. But I was moving,” he said. “But I wasn’t getting anywhere. I don’t know if something made a sound, or if something moved, but that’s what happened to me,” he said.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: I can’t really say it can’t happen, because even in the Bible, it talks about things that existed like that. There was people who could do strange works. But as for us, we don’t rely on that, but it has existed for a long time, different things. But as for me, that’s about all I can say about that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: We’re gonna finish now, I’m going to ask you this last thing. This way that we’re talking in Cherokee, what do you think is going to happen?

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: As for me, I think this way of talking is going to come to an end. It would be great if it doesn’t happen. They’re doing as much as they can, teaching, but also, it has to begin at home.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Truly.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: And if it doesn’t begin there, for instance this younger generation, they don’t speak Cherokee, but if one is learning and if they learn, and there’s five or six more that didn’t, that’s still not worth anything. Family, that’s it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They didn’t set us down and say this is how you speak Cherokee.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: We learned it by hearing it.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: It’s going in a bad way. Like I said, my uncle Taylor, all the time was seeing what was going to happen. He would be really instructing us of things like that. I guess he was sensing that it was getting that way. I wasn’t sensing anything, but nowadays, I realize what he was talking about.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s what he was talking about.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: He was trying to keep that from happening, so it could move forward. And that would be good, if it could move forward.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s what we think now, is we should’ve listened to what they were talking about. When they were talking a long time ago, I should have took it to heart.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: We’re done, I’m thankful for you, Tom.

segments.speaker: tom-duncan
segments.translation: Me too. I’m glad that we saw each other again.
